title: Right concentration
hookLine: the mind gathered and unified, in the four jhanas (MN 141)

cards: Sunlight falling on a sheet of paper does nothing much. Gather the same sunlight through a magnifying glass, and the paper starts to smoke. Nothing was added.

No extra sun. The light was only collected into one point. Water from a garden hose works the same way: spread into a mist, it barely wets the grass; gathered into a stream, it reaches the far end of the yard.
The eighth and last factor of the eightfold path is about that kind of gathering.

teach.b: In Pali it's samma samadhi. Samadhi is usually explained from a verb meaning to put together, to collect: the mind gathered.
In MN 141, where Sariputta lays out the four noble truths, right concentration is defined simply as the four jhanas, four deepening states of meditative absorption.
The next four days take them one at a time, with the Buddha's own pictures. Today is about the gathering itself, and three things. First, it isn't a strain, not frowning hard at a point.
In the suttas' pictures of the jhanas, the gathered mind is pleasant, even joyful.

teach.h: NOT A STRAIN, AND NEVER ALONE.
teach.b: Second, it's never alone. MN 117 calls it noble right concentration with its supports: the seven factors that come before it. A mind gathered to plan a burglary is gathered, too.
It isn't right concentration. Third, concentration and understanding work as partners.
The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's translation: “Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana.”
Buddhist schools differ on how much concentration a person needs, and how deep.
In Theravada teaching, calm, samatha, and insight, vipassana, are often described as developed together; some teachers stress deep absorption, others a lighter, moment-to-moment steadiness.
Zen and Tibetan schools train the gathered mind in their own ways.

how: Buddhists across schools train concentration in meditation, often on the breath; in Theravada communities it is commonly taught as calm (samatha) alongside insight (vipassana), and Zen and Tibetan schools have their own methods for steadying the mind.

o: the mind gathered and collected in one place
a strained, frowning focus on one point
a trance in which you lose all awareness

games.q: match the words of right concentration.
p: right concentration as the four jhanas

s: right concentration means straining hard at one point
the suttas' pictures of the jhanas describe the gathered mind as pleasant, even joyful.
the Dhammapada pairs meditation with knowledge
without one, no other; with both, near unto Nirvana.
any concentrated mind counts as right concentration
MN 117 sets it among its supports, the seven factors before it.

games.q: you sit for ten minutes and your mind scatters twenty times. what does the path invite?
o: give up: you just can't concentrate
gather it back each time; each gathering is the practice
force it to stay, jaw clenched
games.why: samadhi means gathering, and gathering only happens to something that scattered. twenty returns is twenty pieces of practice.

practice: Choose one place where the breath is clearest, the nostrils or the belly, and let your attention rest there; when it scatters, gather it back gently, the way you'd sweep crumbs into your hand.
Every gathering is the practice, and if you have ten minutes today, this is a good day to use them.

wordCard.voice: Samadhi. Concentration: the mind gathered and unified, the eighth factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit samādhi: from sam + ā + dhā, to put together; the mind collected.

carryVoice: Your line: gathered. Nothing added, only the same light collected into one point. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 141, Saccavibhanga Sutta (right concentration as the four jhanas)
Majjhima Nikaya 117, Mahacattarisaka Sutta (noble right concentration with its supports)
